name: English (Lancaster, north-west England)
variety: Northern English of Lancashire as heard in and around Lancaster: a regional accent of the north-west of England, not the traditional rural dialect; features that belong to other parts of Lancashire are marked as such
sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Volume 2: The British Isles. Cambridge University Press.
Beal, Joan (2004). English dialects in the North of England: phonology. In Schneider et al. (eds.), A Handbook of Varieties of English, volume 1. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Hughes, Arthur; Trudgill, Peter; Watt, Dominic (2012). English Accents and Dialects. 5th edition. London: Hodder Education.
Shorrocks, Graham (1998). A Grammar of the Dialect of the Bolton Area. Part I: Introduction, Phonology. Frankfurt: Peter Lang.
Cruttenden, Alan (1997). Intonation. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
contrasts: no FOOT-STRUT split: STRUT words have the vowel of FOOT, /ʊ/ (put = putt, could = cud)
no TRAP-BATH split: BATH words have the short front vowel of TRAP, /a/ (gas and grass rhyme; ant = aunt); PALM and START have a long vowel, so that Sam and psalm differ by length
FACE and GOAT are long monophthongs /eː/ and /oː/
mainly non-rhotic, with long vowels and centring diphthongs where the spelling has r; rhoticity survives with some, mostly older, speakers in central and east Lancashire
long versus short vowels, more nearly a contrast of pure length than in RP because /a/ and /aː/ are close in quality
lexical stress with reduction of unstressed vowels
allophony: final unstressed happY is a lax [ɪ] or an opener [ɛ]-like vowel
ng is [ŋɡ] in much of Lancashire, above all in the south and centre of the county, also at the end of a word (sing [sɪŋɡ], singer, singing); unstressed -ing is commonly [ɪn]
/h/ is often dropped in informal speech
/l/ is dark in all positions for many Lancashire speakers
/t/ between vowels across a word boundary may be [ɹ] (get off, shut up); /t/ before a consonant or a pause is often a glottal stop
the definite article is reduced to [t] or a glottal stop in traditional speech
/ɹ/ is a postalveolar approximant; linking and intrusive /r/ are used by non-rhotic speakers
PALM and START are a long front [aː]; NURSE is [ɜː], merged with SQUARE in parts of south Lancashire
GOOSE is [uː], fronted for younger speakers; older speakers have the GOOSE vowel in book, cook, look
/p t k/ are aspirated; vowels are shorter before voiceless consonants
unstressed syllables have schwa or [ɪ]; word-final schwa is often open
phonotactics: for non-rhotic speakers /r/ occurs only before a vowel
short vowels need a following consonant in a stressed syllable
where ng is [ŋɡ], [ŋ] is only the form of /n/ before a velar stop and not a separate phoneme

stress.rule: As in other accents of English: fixed for each word, with Germanic initial stress and weight-sensitive Latinate stress.
stress.cues: pitch movement on accented syllables, duration, loudness and vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong, as in other accents of England, with schwa and [ɪ] in unstressed syllables; prefixes such as con-, ex-, ad- more often keep a full vowel than in RP
rhythm.notes: I know of no nPVI value for this accent.

length.notes: Long monophthongs /iː uː eː oː aː ɔː ɜː/ contrast with short vowels. No long consonants.

intonation.declarative: falling nuclear tone on the last accented word, ending low
intonation.yes_no_question: rise on the nucleus, or a fall
intonation.continuation: rise or fall-rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.notes: No study of Lancaster intonation is known to me. The rising statement tunes described for some northern cities (Cruttenden 1997) are reported for Liverpool, Tyneside, Glasgow, Belfast and Birmingham, not for Lancaster.

phonation: glottal replacement of /t/ before consonants and pause

problems: STRUT and FOOT are both labelled [ʊ] but use different formant files (vowel/o-_2 and vowel/uu), so a small difference of quality remains where the accent has one vowel
[ŋɡ] is produced only before a vowel (singing is [sɪŋɡɪn]); before a pause or a consonant the plain [ŋ] is used
/l/ is clear before vowels as in RP
there is no h-dropping, no glottal replacement of /t/ and no [ɹ] for /t/
the voice is fully non-rhotic; the remaining rhoticity of Lancashire cannot be chosen
the tunes are the default English ones, and wh-questions get the rising question tune
good: STRUT has the FOOT vowel (strut [stɹʊt], butter [bʊtə])
FACE and GOAT are monophthongs [eː] and [oː]
final unstressed happY is lax [ɪ] and unstressed -ing is [ɪn]
MOUTH starts with a front vowel [æʊ]

notes: eSpeak NG names this voice after Lancaster; its phoneme table (en-n) is a general northern English one. I give no formant, voice onset time or duration values because I know of no published measurements for this accent that I can quote.
